books.section: Topic 1.4 Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest
The Early Colonial Era: Spain Colonizes the New World

primary_sources: Bartolome de las Casas, A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies (1542, published 1552)

parts.modelAnswer: Las Casas wrote to persuade the Spanish crown to stop the cruelty of the encomienda system. He wanted the king to end the forced labor that was destroying Indigenous peoples.
parts.prompt: Identify Las Casas's purpose in writing this account.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for naming Las Casas's purpose, such as persuading the crown to end forced labor or to reform the encomienda system.
scoring.notEarned: Stating only that Las Casas described the Indies, with no purpose named, does not earn the point.

parts.modelAnswer: By calling them gentle and obedient, Las Casas presents them as peaceful people who did not deserve violent conquest. That picture makes Spanish cruelty look unjust, which strengthens his plea for reform.
parts.prompt: Explain how Las Casas's description of Indigenous peoples supports his argument.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining how the description supports the argument, such as by making the victims seem peaceful and the cruelty unjust.
scoring.notEarned: Restating the description with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

parts.modelAnswer: Las Casas wrote to persuade, not to count, so his figures may exaggerate the loss to strengthen his case. Historians therefore check his numbers against other records, which also show a catastrophic decline but not always his exact figures.
parts.prompt: Explain one reason a historian might question the population figures Las Casas gives.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining one accurate reason to question the figures, such as Las Casas writing to persuade, or the lack of a census behind his numbers.
scoring.notEarned: Stating only that the numbers are large, with no reason to question them, does not earn the point.

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Bartolome de las Casas, A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies (written 1542, published 1552). Las Casas wrote that the peoples of Hispaniola were gentle and obedient, owning little, and that the Spanish fell upon them like wolves, killing them and forcing them into hard labor. He claimed the Indigenous population of Hispaniola had fallen from about three million to only two hundred, and he sent the account to Prince Philip of Spain to persuade the crown to stop the cruelty.
